parameters.subject: The 38.9% land gap, and the catch
parameters.text:

parameters.subject: The bill cash quietly pays every year
parameters.text:
=Hi {{ $('Config').item.json.name }},

Most allocators I speak with hold a meaningful balance in cash or short bonds right now. It earns a little, it feels safe, and it waits for a clearer signal before committing to a hard asset. Safe is the word worth pausing on.

Three forces are quietly compounding underneath that balance while it sits.

Inflation, first. MAS and MTI project core inflation of about 1.5 to 2.5 percent for 2026, with the bias to the upside. Idle cash gives up close to that in real terms every year, with no statement that ever shows the loss.

Replacement cost, second. The Singapore Contractors Association reports building material prices up about 20 percent. A home standing today cannot be rebuilt for what it cost a few years ago, and that rising floor sits under everything already built.

Pipeline, third. BCA projects about S$47 to 53 billion of construction contracts in 2026 alone, across more than ten mega projects including Changi T5, Tuas Port, the North South Corridor, the Jurong Region Line and the Cross Island Line. A multi year build programme is one of the cleaner signals of sustained housing and rental demand in the precincts it reaches.

Now the honest caveat a sharp reader is already forming. None of this lifts the price of one specific home. It sets a floor under the asset class, not a guarantee under a single unit. Which unit, which location, which entry price, that is the real work, and it is exactly what a quiet conversation is for.

If it would help to read your own position against this backdrop, I keep a few free 30 minute private sessions open each week, no obligation: {{ $('Config').item.json.calendlyUrl }}.

parameters.subject: Same MRT stop, two land prices
parameters.text:
=Hi {{ $('Config').item.json.name }},

Let me put the question you are already holding on the table. If Lentor Gardens looks underpriced, where is the catch? Land that cheap usually hides a defect.

Here is the honest answer. It is not a flaw, it is timing.

Land is bought years before a home is sold, and your launch price is anchored to what the ground cost back then. Kingsford secured this site at about S$920 psf ppr. The adjacent Lentor Central plot, won later by GuocoLand, cost S$1,278 psf ppr. Same MRT stop, two land prices, a 38.9 percent gap. Nothing is wrong here. The two parcels simply transacted at different moments in the cycle.

That gap does not stay buried. On GuocoLand's higher basis, analysts project the next launch must break even near S$2,378 psf just to make commercial sense. Lentor Gardens carries an indicative average near S$2,250 psf, inside an indicative S$2,100 to S$2,400 band. Every figure here is indicative, with official pricing on 4 July.

So you are not buying a low number. You are buying the distance between two land costs, fixed before either building rose.

One caveat I keep in front of you, never behind. This is primarily a capital and progression play. The yields here are moderate, not spectacular.

The clean way to read this is against your own cost basis and exit math. In a free 30 minute private session I will walk your numbers through that gap with you, before pricing firms up on 4 July. You can book a time that suits you here: {{ $('Config').item.json.calendlyUrl }}.

parameters.subject: Two quiet questions before 4 July
parameters.text:
=Hi {{ $('Config').item.json.name }},

Picture the gallery on 4 July. You like a stack. The agent asks which bedroom and what budget, and you realise two things were never settled in private. Am I paying too much near a top. And can I actually carry this once I want it.

Better to answer both now, calmly, than under bright lights with a queue forming behind you.

On overpaying, the evidence leans the other way. Six neighbours on this exact MRT stop sold roughly 91 to 100 percent: Lentor Modern, Lentor Hills, Hillock Green, Lentoria, Lentor Mansion and Lentor Central Residences. This cluster did not clear once by chance, it cleared again and again. And the adjacent Lentor Central parcel was tendered at S$1,278 psf ppr against Lentor Gardens land near S$920, a 38.9 percent gap. The next launch is projected to break even close to S$2,378 psf, which is why today's indicative working average near S$2,250 psf reads underpriced rather than toppy. Official pricing releases 4 July.

One honest note on history. Buyers in the 2022 Mayflower and Lentor launches realised roughly 13 to 27 percent gains by 2026 over about 3.3 to 3.7 years. Those are past, realised outcomes of other projects. Past performance is not indicative of future results, and nothing here is promised for Lentor Gardens. I show the range so you can weigh it, not lean on it.

On carrying it, indicative entry: a 2 bedroom from about S$1.32m suggests roughly S$8,800 monthly income and S$369k cash plus CPF. A 3 bedroom from about S$1.87m suggests about S$12,500 income and S$521k cash plus CPF.

parameters.subject: Which line is yours, decided early
parameters.text:
=Hi {{ $('Config').item.json.name }},

Most buyers arrive at a launch thinking about which project. The ones who do well arrive thinking about which line. On 18 July, balloting day, that distinction decides everything.

Lentor Gardens is deliberately a smaller unit project. Of about 499 to 502 homes, two bedrooms make up 252 units at 50.2 percent, sized about 60 to 68 sqm. Three bedrooms add 139 units at 27.7 percent, about 81 to 94 sqm. Four bedrooms are the scarce tier, 105 units at 20.9 percent, about 110 to 126 sqm. There are also three strata terraces and three shops.

This is not an accident of design. URA projects Singapore households getting smaller and more numerous, and this mix is built straight for that demand curve. For an investor, the two and three bedroom band is where the broadest future tenant and resale pool sits. For an own stay upgrader, the four bedroom tier is genuinely scarce at one in five, which changes how early you need to decide.

On the plans themselves, the design is unusually efficient. The published layouts run on a dumbbell principle that keeps the bedrooms apart for privacy, the master takes a king bed and the common rooms a queen, with separated kitchen alcoves, dedicated study nooks and very little wasted corridor. The full floor plans by stack release with the official e brochure, and I can send you the complete set the moment they are out.

The part a brochure cannot give you is stack. Orientation, floor band, the view that holds value, the lines that ballot out first. Indicative two bedroom pricing starts near S$1.32m and three bedroom near S$1.87m, with official pricing on 4 July, so the homework is best done before the queue forms, not inside it.

If you would like to walk the mix and pre shortlist the stacks that fit your goal and budget, that is exactly what a quiet session is for. Book a free 30 minutes here and we map your shortlist before 18 July: {{ $('Config').item.json.calendlyUrl }}.

parameters.subject: Who actually rents this, honestly
parameters.text:
=Hi {{ $('Config').item.json.name }},

The capital case for Lentor Gardens is the loud one. The rental case is quieter, and an honest landlord wants it before, not after, keys.

Start with who rents here. The northern catchment is deepening in a way that matters for tenant demand. By 2029 the North South Corridor compresses the drive into the city. The Woodlands Regional Centre, about 700,000 sqm of commercial space anchored by the RTS Link to Johor, pulls a working population north. Closer in, Seletar Aerospace hosts names like Rolls Royce and Pratt and Whitney, with Ang Mo Kio industrial and Nanyang Polytechnic minutes away. That is the employment base your future tenant is drawn from, and Lentor MRT on the Thomson East Coast Line runs them straight to Orchard and Marina Bay in one ride.

Now the number, with its ceiling stated plainly. Lentor Modern, the established neighbour on this exact stop, shows a gross yield band around 3.5 percent. That is solid and real, and it is not spectacular. Past performance is not indicative of future results. I would never sell this as a high yield play, because it is not one. It is a capital and progression asset that also rents to a thickening tenant pool.

The honest work is matching a specific unit, entry price and likely rent to your own holding plan and cash flow tolerance. A spreadsheet cannot weigh that against your portfolio. A quiet conversation can.
